cases.diagnosis: Depression with Executive Dysfunction (Adult ADHD Comorbid)
cases.presenting_complaint: Chronic difficulty focusing, procrastination, and low mood related to work failures
cases.associated: Depression symptoms: Low mood, guilt about underachievement, social withdrawal, sleep disturbance. ADHD symptoms (lifelong): Difficulty sustaining attention, always late, lost jobs due to missing deadlines, messy home/car, starts projects but never finishes, difficulty listening in conversations, forgets appointments, impulsive decisions
cases.risk_factors: Undiagnosed ADHD childhood, academic underachievement despite average intelligence, job instability, recent firing from job he liked, family history (brother with ADHD), childhood enuresis
cases.mse: Appearance: Casual, slightly disheveled. Behavior: Fidgety, difficulty sitting still. Speech: Normal rate, tangential at times. Mood: 'Frustrated, I'm a failure'. Affect: Mildly depressed, anxious. Thought: Negative self-evaluation, no psychosis. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Attention impaired, working memory poor. Insight: Partial - aware of attention issues but didn't connect to ADHD
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 13/27. Adult ADHD screening (ASRS): 21/24 (positive). IQ assessment: Average (FSIQ 98). No learning disability
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. Depression related to untreated ADHD causing functional impairment. No active SI, good insight emerging
cases.explanation: Undiagnosed Adult ADHD commonly presents with secondary depression. ADHD symptoms (inattention, executive dysfunction) lead to academic/work failure, relationship problems, and low self-esteem, which precipitate depression. Correct diagnosis is crucial - treating ADHD often improves mood. This patient likely had ADHD since childhood (symptoms before age 12, per history) but was never diagnosed. Depression is secondary to chronic ADHD-related dysfunction. Co-occurrence is common (20-30% of adults with ADHD have major depression)
cases.management: (1) Assess for ADHD formally - use ASRS, Conners, collateral history; (2) If ADHD confirmed: start stimulant (e.g., methylphenidate 10mg titrating up) or non-stimulant (atomoxetine); (3) ADHD treatment often improves mood without separate antidepressant; (4) If depression persists after ADHD treated: add SSRI; (5) Psychoeducation about ADHD and its impact; (6) CBT for adult ADHD - skill building, organization; (7) Coaching strategies; (8) Address self-esteem and failure beliefs; (9) Workplace accommodations if returning to work; (10) Family education; (11) Long-term management of ADHD; (12) Follow-up monthly initially

cases.diagnosis: Depression in Osteoporosis Patient on Steroids
cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood and fatigue since starting long-term steroids for rheumatoid arthritis 5 months ago
cases.associated: Insomnia (steroid-induced), mood swings, increased appetite, weight gain (8kg), anxiety about appearance changes (moon face), withdrawal from social activities due to embarrassment, anhedonia, bone pain limiting activity
cases.risk_factors: Long-term prednisolone 10mg daily for RA, previous history of depression (post-menopausal), reduced mobility due to arthritis, body image concerns, fear of falling (osteoporosis), social isolation
cases.mse: Appearance: Cushingoid features (moon face), overweight. Behavior: Anxious about appearance. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'I don't recognize myself anymore'. Affect: Depressed, self-conscious. Thought: Preoccupation with appearance, no psychosis. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Insomnia-related concentration issues. Insight: Good
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, cortisol suppressed (expected on steroids), Hb normal, vitamin D low. PHQ-9: 12/27 (mild-moderate). DEXA scan: T-score -2.5 (osteoporosis). Bone density stable on treatment
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation, but body image distress significant. Monitor for steroid-induced psychiatric effects
cases.explanation: Glucocorticoids can cause psychiatric side effects including depression, anxiety, insomnia, and mood swings (steroid-induced mood disorder). Prevalence of psychiatric symptoms on long-term steroids is 15-60%. This patient has steroid-induced insomnia contributing to depression, plus body image distress from Cushingoid changes compounding mood. Social withdrawal worsens depression. Steroid dose is moderate (10mg prednisolone) but duration significant. Managing steroid-induced depression requires balancing psychiatric and rheumatological needs
cases.management: (1) Liaise with rheumatologist regarding steroid-sparing agents (DMARDs, biologics) to reduce steroid dose; (2) Sleep hygiene for steroid insomnia; (3) Short-term low-dose benzodiazepine for severe insomnia if needed; (4) SSRI for depression (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg); (5) Address body image concerns: normal adjustment reaction, counseling; (6) Social engagement despite appearance changes; (7) Support group for RA/osteoporosis; (8) Exercise as tolerated for mood and bone health; (9) Vitamin D and calcium optimization; (10) Monitor for steroid-induced mania/psychosis (rare but possible at higher doses); (11) Regular psychiatric review

cases.presenting_complaint: Widespread pain, fatigue, and low mood for 2 years with recent worsening
cases.duration: Pain symptoms: 2 years. Depression worsening: 3 months
cases.associated: Widespread musculoskeletal pain (9/10), tender points positive, severe fatigue, sleep non-restorative, morning stiffness, cognitive difficulties ('fibro fog'), anhedonia, hopelessness about chronic pain, reduced activity due to pain, relationship strain
cases.risk_factors: Fibromyalgia diagnosis 2 years ago, previous history of depression (age 35), physical abuse in childhood, multiple stressors, job requiring physical labor, poor sleep hygiene
cases.mse: Appearance: Shows pain behaviors, appears tired. Behavior: Reluctant to move, guarded. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'The pain controls my life'. Affect: Depressed, frustrated. Thought: Catastrophic thinking about pain, hopelessness. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Reports 'fibro fog' - poor concentration and memory. Insight: Good - knows pain and depression interact
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, ESR/CRP normal (rules out inflammatory arthritis), B12 normal, vitamin D low. PHQ-9: 18/27. Widespread Pain Index: 14/19. Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire: 68/100 (severe)
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Chronic pain with disability, hopelessness about treatment, passive SI. Chronic pain increases suicide risk
cases.explanation: Depression and chronic pain have bidirectional relationship - 30-60% of chronic pain patients have depression, and depression worsens pain perception. Fibromyalgia is a central sensitization syndrome with widespread pain, fatigue, and cognitive symptoms ('fibro fog'). This patient has comorbid major depression and fibromyalgia with bidirectional worsening. Chronic pain patients often have 'pain catastrophizing' (magnification of pain threat, rumination, helplessness). Treatment requires integrated approach addressing both conditions simultaneously
cases.management: (1) Multimodal treatment: SSRI or SNRI for both conditions (duloxetine or milnacipran FDA-approved for fibromyalgia); (2) Low-dose tricyclic antidepressant (amitriptyline 10-25mg) for sleep and pain; (3) Gabapentin or pregabalin for neuropathic pain component; (4) Physical therapy with gradual exercise program; (5) CBT for pain management and depression; (6) Mindfulness-based stress reduction; (7) Sleep hygiene; (8) Address childhood trauma (contributes to both conditions); (9) Pacing and activity scheduling; (10) Support groups for fibromyalgia; (11) Consider if other causes of chronic pain (rule out inflammatory arthritis); (12) Realistic goal-setting

cases.diagnosis: Depression with Suicidal Ideation - High Risk Assessment
cases.presenting_complaint: Acute worsening of depression with active suicidal ideation following relationship breakup
cases.duration: Current depressive episode: 6 weeks. Breakdown: 1 week ago
cases.associated: Severe low mood, anhedonia, guilt about relationship failure, passive and active suicidal ideation (thoughts of overdose with tablets, has identified specific pills), hopelessness, social isolation, reduced food intake, stopped attending college
cases.risk_factors: Recent romantic relationship breakup (4 days ago), previous suicide attempt at age 19 (overdose), family history of suicide (paternal uncle completed suicide at 35), alcohol use (binge drinking 2-3 times/week), recent academic stress, social media comparison, limited coping skills
cases.mse: Appearance: Disheveled, tearful, appears tired. Behavior: Anxious, restless. Speech: Normal rate but emotional. Mood: 'I can't cope, I want to end it'. Affect: Depressed, anxious. Thought: Active SI with method (overdose, identified tablets), feels worthless, hopelessness. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Oriented, concentration impaired. Insight: Good - knows she needs help
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, ethanol level negative (not currently intoxicated). PHQ-9: 22/27 (severe). Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS): High risk - active ideation with intent and plan
cases.suicide_risk: HIGH RISK. Active suicidal ideation with identified method (overdose), means available (tablets in home), previous attempt, recent precipitant (breakup), impulsivity risk (alcohol use), family history of suicide. Requires immediate safety planning
cases.explanation: This patient presents with acute suicide risk following relationship breakup. High-risk features: active ideation with specific plan and means, previous attempt, family history of suicide, recent precipitant, alcohol use (increases impulsivity), social isolation. Protective factors: good insight, seeking help, no current intoxication. Assessment using Columbia Protocol (C-SSRS) confirms high risk. Safety planning is essential - involves collaborative risk assessment, means restriction, coping strategies, and emergency contacts
cases.management: IMMEDIATE: (1) Comprehensive suicide risk assessment (C-SSRS); (2) Safety planning: written plan with coping strategies, warning signs, emergency contacts, crisis hotline number; (3) MEANS RESTRICTION: remove/access tablets (family member to secure medications); (4) Notify family/close friend - involve in safety planning; (5) Consider brief admission or crisis house if risk too high for outpatient; (6) Ensure not left alone initially. TREATMENT: (7) Start SSRI (sertraline 50mg) - warn 2-4 week lag; (8) Short-term benzodiazepine for acute anxiety if needed; (9) Intensive follow-up (daily contact first week); (10) CBT for suicide prevention; (11) Address alcohol use; (12) Academic accommodations; (13) Social engagement; (14) Long-term therapy for attachment issues and coping skills; (15) Family psychoeducation

cases.diagnosis: Depression in Diabetes Mellitus - Poor Glycemic Control
cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood and poor self-care for 4 months despite worsening diabetes
cases.associated: Poor medication adherence (forgetting doses), overeating comfort foods, stopped exercising, HbA1c 9.8% (worsened from 7.5%), fatigue, sleep disturbance, withdrawal from diabetes support group, believes 'why bother, complications will happen anyway'
cases.risk_factors: Type 2 diabetes for 10 years, recent development of diabetic retinopathy, poor glycemic control, social isolation (wife died 2 years ago), sedentary lifestyle, limited health literacy
cases.mse: Appearance: Obese, appropriate dress. Behavior: Engages but seems hopeless. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'What's the point of controlling sugar if I'm going to go blind anyway'. Affect: Depressed, resigned. Thought: Catastrophic thinking about complications, hopelessness, no active SI but 'if complications happen, I don't want to live like that'. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Mild cognitive complaints (could be diabetes-related). Insight: Partial - knows he's not caring for himself
cases.investigations: Blood: HbA1c 9.8% (poor control), TSH normal, B12 normal, lipids elevated. PHQ-9: 15/27. Kidney function: microalbuminuria present. Eye exam: background retinopathy
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Passive SI linked to fear of disability from diabetes complications. Hopelessness about prognosis increases risk
cases.explanation: Depression is twice as common in diabetics as general population, and depression worsens glycemic control through behavioral (poor adherence, inactivity) and biological (stress hormones) mechanisms. This patient shows 'diabetes distress' - emotional burden of living with chronic illness, which is distinct from but related to depression. Hopelessness about complications is driving both depression and poor self-care. Fear of retinopathy progression is realistic but catastrophized. Intervention is crucial as depression in diabetes increases cardiovascular mortality and complication rates
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg) - also may have modest glycemic benefits; (2) Address diabetes distress alongside depression; (3) Psychoeducation about depression-diabetes cycle; (4) Simplify medication regimen (once-daily if possible); (5) Involve diabetes educator; (6) Connect with peer support for diabetics; (7) Address isolation - reconnect with support group; (8) Behavioral activation for exercise and diet; (9) CBT for catastrophic thinking about complications; (10) Manage retinopathy - ophthalmology follow-up; (11) Coordinate care with endocrinologist; (12) Family involvement for support; (13) Realistic hope - good diabetes control prevents progression

cases.presenting_complaint: Chronic depression with flashbacks, emotional dysregulation, and relationship difficulties
cases.duration: Current exacerbation: 3 months. Chronic symptoms: 10+ years
cases.associated: Current: Low mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, guilt. Chronic trauma symptoms: Flashbacks to childhood abuse, nightmares, hypervigilance, emotional numbing, difficulty trusting others, avoidance of intimacy, self-harm (historical), difficulties with emotional regulation, relationship instability, feeling 'damaged'
cases.risk_factors: Childhood sexual abuse (ages 5-11 by relative), parental neglect, multiple perpetrators, no previous treatment for trauma, recent anniversary of abuse disclosure, current relationship stress (partner triggered trauma responses), social isolation
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately dressed but appears tense. Behavior: Hypervigilant (checks doors, windows), startles easily. Speech: Normal but pauses when discussing trauma. Mood: 'Broken, can't have normal relationships'. Affect: Depressed, restricted, some numbing evident. Thought: Negative self-concept ('damaged goods'), trauma-related cognitions. Perception: No current hallucinations but flashbacks during interview. Cognition: Preserved. Insight: Good - connects current issues to trauma
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 19/27. CAPS-5 (Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale): Positive for PTSD. Personality assessment: features of complex trauma
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate-high risk. History of self-harm, chronic trauma, current relationship stress, passive SI during flashbacks. Complex PTSD increases suicide risk
cases.explanation: Complex PTSD (C-PTSD) results from prolonged, repeated trauma (e.g., childhood abuse) with additional symptoms beyond standard PTSD: emotional dysregulation, negative self-concept, and interpersonal difficulties. This patient meets criteria for both Major Depression and C-PTSD. Flashbacks and trauma memories are being triggered by anniversary and current relationship, worsening depression. Self-harm was likely a coping mechanism for overwhelming trauma-related emotions. Treatment requires trauma-focused therapy but must stabilize depression first. Need to distinguish C-PTSD from BPD - both have emotional dysregulation but C-PTSD has clear trauma etiology and specific trauma-related symptoms
cases.management: (1) Stabilize depression: SSRI (sertraline 50-100mg) - also helps PTSD symptoms; (2) Address acute crisis - safety planning, coping strategies for flashbacks; (3) Phase-based trauma treatment: (a) Safety and stabilization (DBT skills for emotion regulation), (b) Trauma processing (EMDR or trauma-focused CBT), (c) Integration and rehabilitation; (4) Avoid premature trauma processing - can destabilize; (5) DBT for emotion regulation and distress tolerance; (6) Consider inpatient if acute destabilization; (7) Address anniversary reactions; (8) Process relationship triggers; (9) Work on negative self-concept; (10) EMDR after stabilization; (11) Long-term psychotherapy; (12) Consider dissociation - may need adapted treatment; (13) Family/couples therapy if appropriate; (14) Peer support for survivors

cases.diagnosis: Depression in Shift Worker (Circadian Rhythm Disruption)
cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood, sleep problems, and fatigue since starting night shifts 8 months ago
cases.associated: Difficulty sleeping during day (only 4-5 hours despite being off night shifts), excessive sleepiness during night shifts, mood swings, reduced enjoyment of family time, relationship strain (always tired when home), increased caffeine and energy drink use, appetite changes, weight gain
cases.risk_factors: Night shift work (10pm-6am) for 8 months, previous history of seasonal depression, morning chronotype forced into night schedule, poor sleep hygiene on off days, social isolation (friends work day shifts), family history of mood disorder
cases.mse: Appearance: Looks tired, caffeinated. Behavior: Slightly irritable, fatigued. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Exhausted and miserable'. Affect: Mildly depressed, irritable. Thought: No psychosis. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Reports poor concentration and memory. Insight: Good - suspects shift work related
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, vitamin D low (limited sun exposure). PHQ-9: 13/27. Sleep diary confirms circadian disruption. Shift Work Sleep Disorder diagnosis likely
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation. Distress related to sleep disruption and lifestyle impact
cases.explanation: Shift Work Sleep Disorder involves circadian rhythm disruption causing insomnia and excessive sleepiness. Night shift workers have 30-40% higher risk of depression, likely due to: circadian misalignment affecting serotonin/melatonin, social isolation, sleep deprivation, and reduced light exposure. This patient's chronotype (morning type) makes night shifts particularly difficult. His previous seasonal depression suggests circadian vulnerability. Treatment requires addressing both sleep disorder and depression. Light therapy and melatonin can help realign circadian rhythm
cases.management: (1) Discuss with employer about shift rotation or day shift if possible; (2) Sleep hygiene for daytime sleep: dark room, cool temperature, earplugs, consistent schedule; (3) Strategic light exposure: bright light during night shifts, dark glasses on way home; (4) Melatonin 1-3mg 2 hours before desired daytime sleep; (5) Consider dawn simulation; (6) SSRI for depression (e.g., sertraline 50mg); (7) Limit caffeine, especially after midnight; (8) Scheduled naps before night shifts; (9) Family schedule adaptation; (10) Vitamin D supplementation; (11) Exercise on off days; (12) If no improvement, consider shift change; (13) Psychoeducation about circadian rhythms

cases.presenting_complaint: Severe low mood and social withdrawal, with lifelong fear of social situations
cases.duration: Depression: 4 months. Social anxiety: Lifelong, worsening
cases.associated: Depression: Low mood, anhedonia, passive SI, hopelessness. Social anxiety: Fear of judgment, avoids speaking in meetings, limited friends, declined promotion due to public speaking requirement, isolated at home, physical symptoms in social situations (sweating, trembling), self-critical after social interactions
cases.risk_factors: Shy/withdrawn temperament from childhood, bullying during school years, limited peer relationships, no previous mental health treatment, recent promotion opportunity declined, social isolation exacerbated by pandemic
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate but appears anxious. Behavior: Fidgety, poor eye contact. Speech: Soft voice, hesitant. Mood: 'I can't change, I'm broken'. Affect: Depressed, socially anxious. Thought: Negative self-evaluation, catastrophic about social situations. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Partial - aware of social anxiety but feels helpless
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 16/27. Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale: 85/121 (severe). No substance use
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Passive SI related to hopelessness about social anxiety, social isolation. No active plan
cases.explanation: Comorbid Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) and depression is common (up to 50% of SAD patients have depression). Social isolation from SAD leads to loneliness, which precipitates and maintains depression. Depression then worsens social anxiety through negative self-concept and withdrawal. This patient has lifelong SAD with increasing impairment (declined promotion) leading to current depressive episode. Treatment must address both - SSRI helps both conditions, CBT should target both social anxiety (exposure, cognitive restructuring) and depression (behavioral activation)
cases.management: (1) SSRI first-line for both conditions (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg, or paroxetine); (2) CBT targeting both: social skills training, exposure hierarchy for social situations, cognitive restructuring of negative beliefs; (3) Gradual behavioral activation despite anxiety; (4) Consider exposure therapy for public speaking specifically; (5) Social skills group if available; (6) Address missed promotion opportunity; (7) Job counseling - can address public speaking in role; (8) Online/social support groups; (9) Mindfulness for anxiety; (10) Family involvement; (11) Long-term treatment; (12) Realistic goals - may not become extravert but can reduce impairment

cases.diagnosis: Depression Secondary to Vitamin D Deficiency
cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood, fatigue, and body aches for 6 months with recent worsening
cases.associated: Persistent low energy limiting daily activities, diffuse body aches and joint pain, sleep disturbance (non-restorative), mild low mood not typical for her, reduced appetite, hair loss, decreased motivation, symptoms worse in winter months
cases.risk_factors: Office job with minimal sun exposure, vegan diet (limited vitamin D sources), lives in northern city with limited winter sunlight, dark skin (reduced vitamin D synthesis), limited outdoor activities, previous similar symptoms in winters
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate, appears tired. Behavior: Normal but fatigued. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Just no energy to enjoy anything'. Affect: Mildly depressed. Thought: No significant negative cognitions. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Mild concentration issues. Insight: Good - noticed seasonal pattern
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, calcium normal. Vitamin D: 12 ng/mL (severely deficient). PTH elevated (secondary hyperparathyroidism). PHQ-9: 11/27 (mild). Ferritin normal. Lipids normal
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation. Symptoms likely primarily due to vitamin D deficiency
cases.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency is common in India despite sunny climate - risk factors include: indoor lifestyle, dark skin, air pollution blocking UVB, vegetarian/vegan diets, and geographical location. Severe deficiency (<20 ng/mL) is associated with depression - proposed mechanisms include: vitamin D's role in neurotransmitter synthesis (serotonin, dopamine), anti-inflammatory effects, and circadian regulation. This patient has severe deficiency with mild depressive symptoms and prominent fatigue/aches. Correction may improve mood substantially, but may not resolve completely if depression has developed independently
cases.management: (1) Vitamin D replacement: loading dose (e.g., 60,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks) then maintenance (1000-2000 IU daily); (2) Recheck vitamin D in 3 months; (3) Expect mood improvement over 4-8 weeks of treatment; (4) If depression persists after vitamin D normalization, consider SSRI; (5) Increase sun exposure: 10-15 minutes midday sun on arms/legs daily; (6) Dietary changes: include fortified foods, consider fish for vitamin D; (7) Address indoor lifestyle; (8) Exercise outdoors when possible; (9) Calcium supplementation if needed; (10) Monitor PTH; (11) Annual vitamin D screening; (12) Psychoeducation about vitamin D-depression link

cases.presenting_complaint: Persistent low mood and fatigue since cardiac bypass surgery 3 months ago
cases.associated: Low mood not present before surgery, fatigue limiting cardiac rehabilitation, reduced appetite, sleep disturbance (pain-related), worry about heart, avoidance of physical activity (fear of cardiac event), loss of independence (依赖 on family), feels like 'burden', anhedonia, guilt about needing care
cases.risk_factors: Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) 3 months ago, intensive care stay (3 days), history of anxiety (health anxiety), no previous depression, limited cardiac rehabilitation attendance, personality traits (independence, difficulty accepting help)
cases.mse: Appearance: Post-surgical, appears frail. Behavior: Reluctant to move, cautious. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'I'm useless now, can't do anything'. Affect: Depressed, anxious. Thought: Health worries, catastrophic thinking about heart, no suicidal ideation. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Partial - recognizes he's limiting himself
cases.investigations: Blood: Hb recovered (was low post-surgery), TSH normal, BNP normal. PHQ-9: 14/27. Cardiac enzymes normal. Echo shows good graft function. Exercise tolerance test: deconditioning only
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation. Depression related to surgical recovery and loss of independence
cases.explanation: Post-CABG depression affects 20-40% of patients, with onset typically in first 3 months. Risk factors: pre-existing anxiety, ICU stay, pain, reduced independence, and concerns about mortality. Depression worsens cardiac outcomes - increased risk of subsequent cardiac events and mortality. This patient has adjustment disorder with depressed mood progressing to major depression, complicated by health anxiety and personality factors around independence. Deconditioning from activity avoidance worsens fatigue. Cardiac rehabilitation with psychological support improves outcomes
cases.management: (1) SSRI (sertraline 50-100mg) - also has cardiovascular safety; (2) Encourage gradual return to cardiac rehabilitation; (3) CBT for health anxiety and adjustment; (4) Address 'cardiac invalidism' - gradual activity reintroduction; (5) Psychoeducation about normal recovery expectations; (6) Family involvement in recovery; (7) Pain management if limiting activity; (8) Address independence concerns; (9) Peer support (cardiac support groups); (10) Coordinate with cardiologist; (11) Monitor for cardiac anxiety; (12) Gradual return to normal activities; (13) Expect 6-12 months for full recovery
